title: Trie: Prefix Search
oneLiner: A tree of characters where every word that shares a prefix shares the path -- so "how many words start with app?" is one walk, not a scan.
keyTakeaway: Each trie node is one character position; its children are keyed by the next character. Store a count on every node of how many words pass through it, and any prefix query is a walk of length L down from the root: O(L), no matter how many words are stored.
explanation:
Autocomplete, spell-checkers and routing tables all ask the same question: which stored strings start with this? A hash set can only answer "is this exact word here?". A list makes you check every word. A trie (from retrieval, usually said "try") is built for prefixes.

Start with an empty root node. To insert a word, walk it one character at a time: if the current node has a child for that character, move into it; if not, create one. Words that share a start (app, apple, apply) share those first nodes and only branch where they differ. If every node also counts how many inserted words passed through it, then answering "how many words start with p" is: walk p's characters from the root. If you fall off (no child for some character), the answer is 0; otherwise it's the count on the node where you stop.

A node is usually a small class holding a dictionary of children (or a 26-slot array for lowercase letters) and an integer count; add an end-of-word flag when you also need exact-match lookups. In this lesson, insert every word, then answer each prefix query in order.

The visualization below inserts four words and shows, after each one, how many new nodes it had to create -- notice how shared prefixes make later words cheap.

visualizationSteps.message: An empty trie: just the root.
Insert "app": nothing shared yet, so all 3 characters get new nodes (highlighted).
Insert "apple": the first 3 characters reuse existing nodes; only 2 new node(s) (highlighted).
Insert "apply": the first 4 characters reuse existing nodes; only 1 new node(s) (highlighted).
Insert "bat": nothing shared yet, so all 3 characters get new nodes (highlighted).
Query "app": walk a → p → p and read that node's count: 3 words (app, apple, apply).

recognitionSignals: The question is about PREFIXES of strings: autocomplete, "starts with", longest common prefix, word search over a dictionary.
Many strings are queried against the same fixed dictionary, so building a structure once up front pays off.
gotchas: Increment the count on EVERY node along the path while inserting, not only on the last one -- otherwise prefix counts only count words that end exactly there.
Falling off the trie partway through a query means 0 matches; don't return the count of the last node you did reach.
The empty prefix matches every word: the root's count (or just the number of words) is the answer.
confusableWith: Hash Map (Fundamentals): a set of words answers exact membership in O(L) too, but has no notion of prefixes -- you'd have to store every prefix of every word to fake it.
Binary Search: sorting the words and binary searching for the prefix range also works (O(L log n) per query); a trie trades memory for skipping the log n.

complexity.note: Here L is the longest word or prefix. Inserting the n words touches up to n · L nodes, and each of the q prefix queries walks at most L characters, so O(n · L + q · L). In the worst case (no shared prefixes) the trie stores a node per character, O(n · L); the q answers are the output.
